title: engine.v1 — the shape of the engine manifest
description: The engine manifest is the one committed file that records what this repository's engine is made of: which engine release it runs, the version of each installed module, and the identity tier that governs how guardrail changes are gated. It is a lockfile-style inventory — the source of truth an upgrade reads to know each module's starting version — and doubles as the operator-readable record of the engine's contents. It lives at .engine/engine.json. This schema governs its shape only.

engine_release.description: The engine release this repository runs, as a version string (for example 1.2.0, or 0.0.0-dev while the engine is still being built). This is the single version an operator sees.

min_upgradeable_from.description: The oldest engine release proven to have a clean one-run upgrade path to this release, as a version string (for example 0.3.2). A deployed engine older than this cannot update cleanly to this release — its own already-shipped update code predates the file-tidying machinery that removes what a release renamed or dropped — so the update refuses cleanly (nothing applied) and routes the operator to stay on their current version, rather than opening a broken pull request. The value pattern is enforced so a malformed floor cannot silently disable the guard. Optional: absent on releases cut before this floor shipped, in which case no floor check runs.

packages.description: Each installed module mapped to its installed version (for example { "core": "1.2.0" }). These per-module versions are internal bookkeeping — the 'from' versions an upgrade reads before it overlays new code — not numbers the operator manages directly.

removed_capabilities.description: The release cut's own inventory of capabilities removed by dropping a WHOLE module — the sibling of a surviving module's manifest-level `retired_capabilities`, kept HERE because a removed module has no manifest left to carry its own notice. Each key is a removed module's id; each value carries the plain-language line the update shows the operator (`description`) and the engine release the removal took effect in (`removed_in`, stamped by the cut). This block does DOUBLE duty: it is the operator-facing explanation AND the release's proof that the module's absence is intentional (not a broken or incomplete release) — which is what authorizes the update to reconcile the module away rather than refuse. Unlike the append-only, version-keyed `retired_capabilities`, this is CURRENT-STATE and keyed by module-id (one entry per removed module): the update announces it while a deployer still holds the module and this release no longer ships it, so no version-range history is needed. An entry accumulates and is never dropped while any supported upgrader could still hold the module (once `removed_in` is at or below `min_upgradeable_from`, no such upgrader remains and the entry may be pruned). Optional: absent on a release that has removed no module, and on releases cut before this block shipped.

description.description: The one plain-language line the update shows the operator — what they could ask the engine for before and no longer can, in operator language (for example 'The engine no longer offers to bring a set-aside note back into search; ask me to search your notes directly instead.'). Authored when the module is removed (via `remove --removal-notice` or by hand); never empty.

removed_in.description: The engine release this removal took effect in, stamped by the release cut when it records the removal. Optional: an entry authored at removal time carries only `description` until the next cut stamps this, so a not-yet-stamped entry is valid.

identity.description: The identity tier governing how the engine's own guardrails may change. solo: a single gate-holder — a guardrail can never weaken silently, but a weakening can still happen with the operator's explicit consent (the engine acts with the operator's credentials). team: a distinct engine identity holds enforcement-admin, so a guardrail cannot weaken at all. This is per-repository and re-chosen at first-run setup; it is not inherited from a template.

handle.description: The operator's own account handle, captured at first-run setup and preserved as operator config. It is the owner the engine writes into the code-ownership block for its own files, so an engine update re-renders that block for the new release's files while keeping this owner. Optional: it is absent until first-run setup derives and records it (and absent in the engine's own home repository, which runs no first-run setup), so a manifest without it stays valid.

default_branch.description: The repository's default branch name, derived from GitHub/git at first-run setup and preserved as operator config. The engine reads it offline to tell whether the operator's top-level checkout is sitting on its main line or has drifted off it, so the check does not depend on a refs/remotes/origin/HEAD that is frequently unset. Optional: absent until first-run setup derives and records it (and absent in the engine's own home repository, which runs no first-run setup), so a manifest without it stays valid.

home_repository.description: The engine's home repository as an owner/repo slug (for example StarshipSuperjam/engine-template) — the single coordinate that is the source of truth for where the engine fetches its own updates from, and for where a fork-native deployment escalates a contribution to. A generated repo is detached from its home (no upstream remote), so the engine updates by pulling that home's tagged GitHub releases, never by a git pull and never from this repo's own origin. Seeded from the template's committed manifest and carried forward at first-run setup; because it selects where executable engine code is fetched from, changing it to a different value is a guardrail-weakening change that needs the operator's explicit acknowledgment. Optional: absent in a repository generated before this coordinate shipped, in which case the engine cannot update and says so plainly rather than guessing a home.

product_repository.description: The repository this engine exists to build and work ON, as an owner/repo slug (for example StarshipSuperjam/engine-template) — the engine's PRODUCT, a DISTINCT coordinate from home_repository (which is where the engine's own code is fetched FROM). Recorded ONLY when the product is a repository DIFFERENT from the one the engine is deployed into (the fork-native / engine-mechanic arrangement of eADR-0026 'external-contribution-fork-native', where self = the deployed-into repo, product = the un-owned upstream it contributes to); when absent, the product IS this repository itself, derived live from the checkout's origin — so a self-building deployment stores nothing and cannot drift stale. INVARIANT (load-bearing): this is a display-only work-target LABEL. Nothing may fetch from, execute against, clone, or issue a GitHub write to this coordinate. A wrong value here can only mislabel a status line — never fetch or run code, which is exactly why (unlike home_repository) changing it is not a guardrail-weakening act. Giving it any consumer that fetches/executes/writes would inherit home_repository's supply-chain and command surface and is a re-classification event that must go back through the engine's guardrail-weakening analysis (eADR-0011) before it ships. Optional: absent on a self-building deployment and in a repository generated before this coordinate shipped.

product_build_target.description: The executable twin of the display-only product_repository, and when set it is the product coordinate that governs (product_repository then need not be set). It is the repository this engine is authorized to BUILD and DELIVER pull requests INTO, as an owner/repo slug (for example StarshipSuperjam/engine-template). This is the engine-mechanic arrangement (eADR-0026): a deployed instance whose product is a repository the operator OWNS, checked out separately on the maintainer's machine, into which the mechanic opens direct pull requests. INVARIANT (load-bearing): UNLIKE product_repository (a display-only label that nothing may act on), this coordinate is EXECUTABLE — the engine may resolve it to branch, commit, and open a GitHub pull request against the matching local checkout — so it inherits home_repository's supply-chain and command surface: a wrong or tampered value redirects where the engine writes and runs code. Therefore SETTING it (absent -> present) OR changing it is a guardrail-weakening act that fires the operator's guardrail-ack (the weakening_guard product_build_target detector, which — unlike the home detector — flags the FIRST recording, because arming a previously-inert engine IS the re-classification event), and a fail-closed belt (mechanic_build.product_checkout_matches) refuses to act unless this slug matches the checkout's own origin. When present it is the SINGLE source of truth for the engine's product: product_repository is then the display label only and need not be set, and boot's orientation prefers this field. Optional: absent on every self-building deployment (the product IS this repository, derived live from origin) and in the engine's own home repository — an absent value is the safe default that records no executable target and keeps the engine building only its own repo.

control_plane.description: What the engine did to this repository's branch protection at setup, recorded so a later clean removal can reverse exactly that and nothing of the operator's. Written by the control-plane apply step on a brownfield arrival (and on greenfield, to record that the engine owns its own ruleset). Optional: absent until the gate is turned on, and on a repo whose protection was already fully in force.

ruleset_mode.description: created: the engine created and owns its own branch-protection ruleset (greenfield). augmented: the engine added its checks into a pre-existing PRODUCT ruleset in place (brownfield), so removal strips back only what it added and never deletes the operator's rule.

augmented_ruleset_id.description: The id of the product ruleset the engine augmented (when ruleset_mode is augmented); null when the engine created its own.

added.description: The exact pieces the engine added to a product ruleset, so removal reverses precisely them: the required-check contexts it unioned in, and any wholly-missing floor rule types it added. null when the engine created its own ruleset.

protection_posture.description: A deliberate, operator-consented record that this repository's GitHub plan cannot host branch-protection rulesets at all, so the standing protection check reports it as an honest, non-blocking warning instead of hard-failing every pull request. Written ONLY by `bootstrap.py accept-unprotected`, which first re-verifies that the branch-rules API genuinely returns GitHub's plan-limitation 403 for this repo — never inferred, never written silently. Its mere presence never softens the gate: the standing check ALSO demands a live plan-limitation 403 at evaluation time, so on any repo whose plan can host protection (the read succeeds there) this record is inert and the check stays hard. Absent on every deployment whose platform can host protection (the default) — and that absence is exactly what keeps the check hard-failing when protection SHOULD be available but is missing or unreadable. The `operator_login`/`recorded_on` fields are an advisory audit breadcrumb of who ran the accept and when — never authenticated proof of consent (a repository whose plan cannot host branch rulesets has no enforced review on the pull request that records this, so the field is a recorded 'by', not a verified one).

status.description: The recorded posture. unsupported-platform: the repository's GitHub plan cannot host branch rulesets (the branch-rules API returns GitHub's plan-limitation 403). An enum-of-one deliberately, leaving room for a future posture without reshaping the block.

reason.description: A short plain-language reason recorded with the acceptance, for the operator reading engine.json later (for example 'This private repository's plan does not expose branch rulesets; the owner accepted running without the protection floor.'). Never empty.

operator_login.description: The GitHub login whose token recorded this decision, read from GET /user at record time — an advisory 'recorded by', the who of the acceptance. It is the token owner, NOT authenticated proof of the operator's consent (the reviewed pull request carrying this block is that); downstream copy presents it as 'recorded by', never as governance evidence.

recorded_on.description: The UTC date the operator accepted the posture (YYYY-MM-DD), which the standing warning and boot's calm line cite. Recorded via the engine's sanctioned clock, not a hand-rolled time idiom.

engine_identity.description: The distinct, non-admin GitHub identity that authors the engine's commits and pull requests in TEAM mode, so the operator becomes the enforced code-owner reviewer — a change cannot merge without a second sign-off, and this identity (holding no admin) cannot itself weaken the ruleset. Recorded when the operator switches solo->team via the team-switch operation; absent in solo (the default) and in the engine's own home repository (which runs no first-run setup), so a manifest without it stays valid. Records only the PUBLIC identity — never a token or any secret, which stays in the operator's own credential store, so switching back to solo simply drops this record.

login.description: The machine-user account's GitHub login (for example 'my-project-engine') — a second account the operator created and added as a non-admin (write) collaborator, whose credential the operator's build sessions authenticate as. Commits and pull requests are attributed to it, and the code-owner review requirement is measured against it.

email.description: The commit-author email for that identity, set into git config so the engine's commits carry it. Optional: the login alone identifies the author; the email is the git-level attribution.
